title: New movements
hookLine: lay movements like Focolare and Sant'Egidio work for unity and peace

cards: Trent, in northern Italy, during the Second World War. The bombs are falling, and a young schoolteacher named Chiara Lubich crowds into an air-raid shelter with a few friends.
They've brought one book, the Gospels, and read it by candlelight, asking what would still stand if everything else fell. They keep landing on Jesus's prayer that his followers may all be one.
Years later in Rome, high school students start meeting to read the Gospel, then going out to the poor on the city's edge. Neither group was started by a bishop or a priest.

teach.b: Chiara's circle became the Focolare movement. Focolare is Italian for hearth, the fire a family gathers around, and that was the idea: small communities living the Gospel together like a family at the fire.
Their key text is Jesus's prayer at the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee."
Focolare took it to heart, building friendships with other Christians, with people of other faiths, and with people of none.
The Roman students, gathered by Andrea Riccardi, took their name, Sant'Egidio, from a small church in the Trastevere neighborhood.

Their life rests on three things: prayer each evening, friendship with the poor, and peace. That last one reached all the way to a war: talks held at their house in Rome helped bring the civil war in Mozambique to an end.
Who leads? These movements are led by laypeople, people who aren't priests or vowed religious, with jobs and families.

The Second Vatican Council taught that the laity share in the Church's mission by their own calling, through baptism, not as helpers on loan from the clergy. Movements like these are one shape that teaching took.
Priests and bishops belong to some of them, but the founders were a teacher and a student.

Look back over the week: a pope greeting the world with peace, a teenager with a website, pilgrims, a church on every continent, a church underground, believers under pressure, and now laypeople leading.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.

how: Catholics join lay movements and associations such as Focolare, Sant'Egidio and the Saint Vincent de Paul Society, meeting for prayer and Scripture and serving the poor, usually alongside their parish life.

games.q: you're a young teacher in an air-raid shelter with a few friends and room to carry one book. what do you bring?
o: a novel to pass the time.
games.why: Chiara Lubich and her friends read the Gospels by candlelight, and kept landing on the prayer that all may be one.

practice: Picture the laypeople already at work where you live: a parish food pantry, a prayer circle in a living room, a Saint Vincent de Paul group collecting coats, a Focolare or Sant'Egidio community, a Catholic Worker house.
Rest your hands in your lap and notice what they could carry for an hour a week. If you pray, ask where they're needed; if you don't, let the question sit quietly.

wordCard.voice: New movements. Communities like Focolare and Sant'Egidio, started and led by laypeople, working for unity, for the poor and for peace.

carryVoice: Your line: laypeople lead. Their calling comes from baptism. See you tomorrow.
